title: Anthropic's $1.5 Billion Copyright Settlement Gets Final Court Approval
excerpt: A federal judge has approved the largest known copyright recovery in U.S. history, resolving authors' claims that Anthropic used pirated books to train its Claude AI chatbot.
body:
• A U.S. federal judge has granted final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement with authors, the largest known copyright recovery in U.S. history.
  • The settlement covers roughly 500,000 book titles, with authors receiving approximately $3,000 per work, and more than 91% of class members have already claimed their share.
  • The judge reduced attorney fees from $187.5 million to $101.6 million, calling the original request a potential "windfall" for lawyers.
  • The case is the first major AI copyright class action to settle, setting a precedent as more than 130 similar lawsuits target other tech companies.

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín on Monday granted final approval to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement of a class action brought by authors who accused the AI company of using pirated books to train its Claude chatbot. The deal is the largest known copyright payout in American history and the first major AI training lawsuit to reach resolution, according to Reuters.

The case was filed in 2024 by novelist Andrea Bartz, journalist Charles Graeber, and writer Kirk Wallace Johnson, who alleged Anthropic mass-downloaded copyrighted books from shadow libraries like LibGen to train its large language models. Anthropic, backed by Amazon and Alphabet, denied wrongdoing but chose to settle rather than face a trial that could have resulted in damages running into hundreds of billions of dollars.

How the Settlement Took Shape

Retired Judge William Alsup laid the groundwork for the deal in June 2025 when he ruled that Anthropic's use of copyrighted books to train Claude qualified as fair use under U.S. law — but only when the copies were lawfully obtained. He found that the company violated authors' rights by storing more than 7 million pirated books in a "central library," regardless of whether all were used for training.

"Anthropic's use of pirated books was not fair."

— Judge William Alsup, in his 2025 ruling

That distinction proved decisive. With a trial set for December 2025 to determine damages, Anthropic agreed to the $1.5 billion fund in September 2025. The settlement covers an estimated 500,000 titles, with distribution favoring books of higher commercial value while providing a flat per-title payment of roughly $3,000 for most works.

Judge Cuts Attorney Fees, Rejects Objections

While approving the deal, Judge Martínez-Olguín sharply reduced the plaintiffs' legal fee request. Class counsel at Susman Godfrey and Lieff Cabraser had initially sought $300 million in fees before withdrawing that bid after judicial pushback. Their revised request of $187.5 million — representing 12.5% of the fund — was still deemed excessive.

The judge awarded approximately $101.6 million, amounting to about 6.8% of the settlement fund. She opted for the "lodestar" method of calculating fees based on hours worked and billing rates, rather than a percentage-based approach, saying the larger award would produce a "windfall" for the lawyers.

"We are gratified by the Court's ruling granting final approval of this historic settlement. It is the largest known copyright recovery in history."

— Justin Nelson, lead attorney for the authors

The judge also overruled objections from some class members who argued the settlement was too small, saying their complaints were "not grounded in a realistic assessment of the overall risks and rewards of a trial."

Wider Implications for AI and Copyright

The settlement arrives at a critical moment for the AI industry. More than 130 copyright lawsuits now target AI developers including OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Nvidia, according to IP CloseUp. The Anthropic case is the first to settle, and its outcome is being closely watched as a benchmark.

Not all authors accepted the deal. Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment and several individual writers opted out, contending that $3,000 per book undervalues their work. Their separate suits continue. Britain's Bloomsbury Publishing, the Harry Potter publisher, confirmed it stands to receive compensation for 14,087 titles covered by the settlement, with proceeds split equally between authors and the publisher, according to Reuters.

Anthropic deputy general counsel Aparna Sridhar noted that the settlement was reached after the court's fair use ruling. "We are pleased that more than 91% of authors and publishers covered by the settlement have claimed their share of the payment," she said.

What Comes Next

The ruling does not resolve the broader legal question of whether training AI models on copyrighted material constitutes infringement. No appellate court has ruled squarely on the issue, and the settlement removes the chance for higher courts to review Alsup's partial summary judgment on fair use.

For Indian authors and publishers with works distributed in the U.S. market, the settlement creates a potential template for future claims. Several major publishing houses have already begun striking licensing deals with AI firms, and the European Union's AI Act now requires transparency about training data — a regulatory approach that could influence India's own evolving digital governance framework.

Pending cases involving Disney, Thomson Reuters, and the consolidated OpenAI litigation carry different facts but face similar legal questions. The pressure on AI companies to license content rather than litigate is building. As one legal analysis noted, the era when AI companies could train on almost anything they downloaded has ended — and the cost of that approach just became quantifiable.
image_caption: Anthropic, the maker of Claude AI, has agreed to pay $1.5 billion to resolve copyright claims by authors. A federal judge granted final approval of the settlement on Monday, marking the largest copyright recovery in U.S. history.
nri_angle: The settlement sets a precedent for how AI companies handle intellectual property globally, affecting Indian authors and publishers whose works may have been used in AI training datasets.
